html:
An agent with thousands of stored memories can't dump all of them into context on every step — it needs to pull back only the handful actually relevant to what it's doing right now. That's retrieval, running at agent time instead of at answer-a-question time: the exact mechanism already covered on the RAG planet, applied to an agent's own memory store instead of a document collection.

You need: Short-Term vs. Long-Term Agent Memory.

The question it answers

"Once an agent has a large memory store, how does it find the few memories actually relevant right now?" The answer is retrieval: embed the current situation into a vector, embed every stored memory the same way, and rank memories by similarity — identical in mechanism to dense retrieval on the RAG planet, just retrieving from a store of the agent's own past facts and experiences instead of a document corpus.

Intuition

A doctor with a thick patient file doesn't re-read the whole file before every question — they pull up the specific entries relevant to today's complaint. Which entries are relevant changes with the question being asked right now, which is exactly why this has to be a retrieval step at the moment it's needed, not something decided once in advance.

Definition and notation

cosine similarity(q, m) = (q · m) / (‖q‖ ‖m‖)
retrieved memories = top-K stored memories by similarity to the current query

A worked example

A query vector against four stored memories, ranked by cosine similarity exactly as on the RAG planet:

query:  "what units does the user want?"           q = (0.8, 0.6)

m1  "the user prefers metric units"                 v = (1, 0)   similarity = 0.800
m2  "the user's deadline is Friday"                 v = (0, 1)   similarity = 0.600
m3  "the user prefers metric and works in km"       v = (1, 1)   similarity = 0.990
m4  "the user prefers imperial units"                v = (-1, 0)  similarity = -0.800

top 2 retrieved: m3 (0.990), m1 (0.800)

m2's deadline fact and m4's directly contradicted preference both score low or negative — exactly what should happen, since neither is relevant to a question about units. The ranking does the filtering automatically; nothing had to specially mark m2 and m4 as irrelevant in advance.

Bench

Interactive bench: Pulling the right memory back out. Rank an agent's stored memories against the current query by cosine similarity.

Try this

  1. Read the ranked list and check that the two memories about units score highest.
  2. Slide K down to 1 and notice which single memory wins.
  3. Imagine the query were instead "when is this due?" — which memory should now score highest, and why does the embedding step have to change for that?

What you should notice: the same similarity mechanism that ranks documents against a question on the RAG planet ranks an agent's own memories against whatever it's currently doing — nothing about retrieval itself changes when the store is memories instead of documents.

Where it appears in AI

  • This is exactly dense retrieval from the RAG planet, applied to a store of the agent's own memories rather than an external document collection — the embedding and ranking mechanism is identical.
  • Memory Compression and Forgetting determines what's even left in the store to retrieve from — a memory that was compressed away or dropped can't be retrieved no matter how relevant it would have been.
  • A RAG pipeline's retrieval step runs once per user question; this runs continuously, at every point in an agent's own task where it needs to recall something relevant to the step it's on.

Common pitfalls

  • Treating memory retrieval as a one-time lookup at the start of a task. Relevance changes as the task progresses — the right memories to retrieve partway through a multi-step task can be completely different from the ones relevant at the start.
  • Retrieving too few memories (missing something relevant) or too many (burying the genuinely relevant ones in noise). K is a real tuning knob here exactly as it is in RAG retrieval generally — there's no single right value independent of the memory store's size and redundancy.
  • Assuming a high similarity score guarantees usefulness. A memory can be topically similar but outdated or contradicted by a more recent one (m4 contradicts m1 directly) — similarity ranks relevance to the query's wording, not correctness or recency on its own.

Quick check

1. In the worked example, why does m3 score higher than m1, even though m1 is also about metric units? m3's vector (1, 1) has a direction closer to the query's (0.8, 0.6) than m1's (1, 0) does — cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors, and m3 happens to point more directly toward the query's direction.
2. Why does m4 score negative instead of just low? m4's vector (-1, 0) points in roughly the opposite direction from the query — it directly contradicts the metric-units preference the query is about, and cosine similarity can go negative exactly when two vectors point in substantially opposite directions.
3. What's the key difference between this topic and retrieval on the RAG planet? The mechanism (embed, rank by cosine similarity, take the top K) is identical — the only difference is what's being retrieved from: the agent's own memory store of facts and past experience, instead of an external document collection.

Key terms

  • Agent-time retrieval: running a retrieval step continuously during an agent's task, rather than once per external question.
  • Memory store: the collection of an agent's embedded past facts and experiences that retrieval ranks against.
  • Top-K: the number of highest-similarity memories actually pulled back for use.
